html:
Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire, in the Orkhon Valley of central Mongolia. Genghis Khan made his base there around 1220, and his son Ögedei built walls and a palace in 1235.

For a few decades it was the place where the world came to the khans. Envoys, merchants and captive craftsmen arrived from China, Persia, Russia and Europe. It had a Muslim quarter and a Chinese quarter, mosques, Buddhist temples and a Christian church.

The Flemish friar William of Rubruck visited in 1254, as told under William of Rubruck in Karakorum. He described a great silver tree made by a captured Parisian goldsmith, which poured wine, mare's milk and other drinks from pipes for the khan's guests. He thought the town itself smaller than the French village of Saint Denis.

When Kublai Khan took power in the 1260s he moved the capital to Khanbaliq, today's Beijing, and Karakorum declined. A Ming army destroyed it in 1388. In 1585 the Buddhist monastery Erdene Zuu was built near the ruins, partly from their stones.
sum: Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire, in the Orkhon Valley of central Mongolia. Genghis Khan made his base there around 1220, and his son Ögedei built walls and a palace in 1235.
